title: Query-Efficient Hard-label Black-box Attack: An Optimization-based Approach (OPT)
authors: Minhao Cheng, Thong Le, Pin-Yu Chen, Jinfeng Yi, Huan Zhang, Cho-Jui Hsieh

pages.title: Turning a label oracle into an optimization problem
pages.subtitle: The OPT attack in one sentence

blocks.html: The Boundary Attack proved that label-only attacks are possible, but it explored the boundary with a blind random walk and paid for it with enormous query counts — often $10^5$ to $10^6$ queries per image. This paper's insight is that the same problem can be written as a clean, continuous optimization problem, after which classic optimization machinery drives the search far more efficiently.

The mental shift is everything. The Boundary Attack asks 'which pixels do I nudge?' and wanders. OPT asks 'in which direction is the boundary closest, and how far is it?' — and then does gradient descent on the answer. The result: the same tiny perturbations as the Boundary Attack, but at roughly 3–4× lower query cost, plus actual convergence guarantees.
Replace the discontinuous label loss with a smooth, real-valued quantity the label oracle can measure: the distance to the decision boundary along a chosen direction.

pages.title: The hard-label setting, and why the obvious approach fails
pages.subtitle: You cannot optimize a step function

blocks.html: Recall the shared hard-label / decision-based threat model that unites this whole family of papers: the attacker submits inputs and sees only the final predicted label — no probabilities, no logits, no gradients. Each query buys exactly one bit: is this point classified the way I want, or not? Success is measured by queries-to-success: how many evaluations to reach a small perturbation norm (usually $\ell_2$).

Now picture why a normal attack collapses here. In white-box land you minimize a smooth loss like the cross-entropy with gradient descent. The hard-label analog — is the label still correct? — is a step function of the input. As you slide an image around, the predicted label stays constant, then suddenly jumps when you cross the boundary.

A step function is poison for optimization on two counts. First, its gradient is zero almost everywhere and undefined at the jump, so there is no slope to descend. Second, you cannot even estimate the gradient by finite differences: probe two nearby points and they almost always return the same label, so the finite difference reads as exactly zero. The optimizer thinks it is on a flat plain when it is actually next to a cliff.

Reading this: $f(x)$ is the hard-label classifier, $y_0$ the true class, and $\mathbb{1}[\cdot]$ the indicator that returns 1 when its condition holds. The loss is flat (gradient zero) everywhere except the boundary, where it has a discontinuous jump. This dead-flat-then-cliff shape is the central obstacle the paper must engineer around.
The whole trick: stop measuring the label directly. Instead measure how far the boundary is along a direction — a quantity that varies smoothly.

pages.title: Optimize the direction, measure the distance
pages.subtitle: From input space to direction space

blocks.html: Here is the reformulation that makes everything work. Stand at the original image $x_0$ and shine a flashlight in some direction $\theta$. Walk along that beam; at some distance the model's label flips. Define $g(\theta)$ as exactly that distance — how far you travel from $x_0$ along $\theta$ before the prediction changes. A small $g(\theta)$ means the boundary is close in that direction, which is exactly where you want to plant a tiny perturbation.

Term by term: $x_0$ is the original image; $\theta/\lVert\theta\rVert$ is the unit direction (the beam); $\lambda$ is the distance traveled; $f(\cdot)$ is the label oracle; $y_0$ the original class. So $g(\theta)$ is the smallest distance $\lambda$ at which the label first becomes wrong. (For a targeted attack, replace $f(\cdot)\neq y_0$ with $f(\cdot)=y_{\text{target}}$ and aim the beam toward a target-class image.)

The entire attack is now this one line: find the direction $\theta^{*}$ whose boundary distance is smallest. That direction gives the smallest adversarial perturbation, with norm $g(\theta^{*})$. The payoff: unlike the raw step-function label loss, $g(\theta)$ is continuous in $\theta$ — rotate the beam a little and the crossing distance moves a little. Now there is a real surface to descend.

Why does this dodge the cliff problem? Because we moved the discontinuity inside $g$. The label still jumps, but it jumps as a function of $\lambda$ along a fixed beam — and we handle that jump with binary search (next page), not with gradients. The outer variable $\theta$ sees only the smooth distance.

pages.title: Measuring g with binary search
pages.subtitle: Extracting a real number from a yes/no oracle

blocks.html: Computing $g(\theta)$ needs nothing but hard labels. Two phases: first bracket the boundary with a coarse outward search, then pin it down with binary search. A worked picture: suppose along direction $\theta$ the label is still correct at $\lambda=1$ but wrong at $\lambda=8$. The boundary lies between 1 and 8.

items: Coarse step: grow $\lambda$ (e.g. double it: 1, 2, 4, 8...) querying the label each time, until it flips — giving a bracket $[\lambda_{\text{lo}}, \lambda_{\text{hi}}]$ with correct label below and wrong label above.
Binary search: query the midpoint; if it is adversarial move $\lambda_{\text{hi}}$ down, else move $\lambda_{\text{lo}}$ up. Each query halves the interval.
Result: a real-valued $g(\theta)$ known to tolerance $\epsilon$ in about $\log_2(\text{range}/\epsilon)$ queries — a handful per evaluation.

blocks.html: This is the crux of how a discontinuous oracle yields a smooth number: binary search converts a sequence of one-bit yes/no answers into a precise distance, at logarithmic cost. The trade-off to remember: every single evaluation of $g$ hides a whole binary search, so $g$ is not free — this is the cost Sign-OPT will later attack.

pages.title: Zeroth-order optimization of the direction
pages.subtitle: Estimating the gradient of g without any gradient

blocks.html: We can evaluate $g(\theta)$ but we have no formula for its gradient (the oracle is a black box). So OPT estimates the gradient the gradient-free way, called zeroth-order optimization: jiggle $\theta$ by a small random vector $u$, measure how $g$ responds, and read that finite difference as the slope in direction $u$.

Term by term: $u_q$ is a random Gaussian direction (a tiny rotation of the beam); $\beta$ is a small smoothing radius; $g(\theta+\beta u_q)-g(\theta)$ asks did rotating toward $u_q$ bring the boundary nearer or push it farther?; dividing by $\beta$ turns that into a slope; multiplying by $u_q$ points the estimate along that direction. Averaging over $Q$ random probes (the paper uses around $Q=20$) cancels noise. The result $\hat{g}$ is an estimated gradient of $g$.

Then take an ordinary gradient-descent step with learning rate $\eta$ and renormalize so $\theta$ stays a unit direction. Iterate until $g(\theta)$ stops shrinking. The final adversarial example is $x_0 + g(\theta^{*})\,\theta^{*}$.

The hidden bill: each of the $Q$ probes per step requires its own binary search to evaluate $g$. That multiplication — $Q$ probes × many bisection queries × many steps — is exactly what Sign-OPT later slashes.

pages.title: Far fewer queries than the random walk
pages.subtitle: OPT versus Boundary Attack, by the numbers

blocks.html: By turning aimless exploration into directed optimization, OPT reaches the same perturbation sizes as the Boundary Attack using roughly 3–4× fewer queries, and it converges in cases where the random walk stalls. On MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet it consistently produces a smaller distortion at any fixed query budget.

Two further wins. (1) It handles targeted attacks cleanly — just initialize the beam toward an image of the target class. (2) It generalizes beyond images: because it only ever queries a label oracle, the same method attacks non-differentiable models such as gradient-boosted decision trees, which white-box and finite-difference score-based attacks cannot touch.

The provable-convergence framing is itself a contribution. Because $g(\theta)$ is a genuine continuous (Lipschitz) objective, the attack inherits the convergence guarantees of zeroth-order stochastic gradient descent — something the heuristic random walk could never claim.

pages.title: Why this paper mattered
pages.subtitle: The reformulation everything else builds on

blocks.html: OPT's lasting gift is the direction-and-distance formulation: $\min_{\theta} g(\theta)$, with $g$ measured by binary search. This single move makes the hard-label problem behave like a smooth optimization and opens it to the whole toolbox of zeroth-order methods. Every later hard-label attack in this collection is a variation on it.

Its remaining bottleneck is the price of each gradient estimate, and the paper is honest about it: every evaluation of $g$ is a binary search, and one gradient step needs $Q$ of them. Sign-OPT removes most of that cost with a sharp observation — to descend, you only need the sign of each directional derivative, not its magnitude, and the sign can be read from a single comparison rather than a full bisection. HopSkipJump takes a different route, estimating the gradient direction at the boundary by Monte-Carlo sampling.
OPT: reformulate the attack as minimizing the distance-to-boundary $g(\theta)$ along a direction, measure that distance by binary search, and optimize $\theta$ with zeroth-order gradients.
